content: In sentinel surveillance, the duration of the surveillance period is determined by the time required to achieve the desired sample size, which is influenced by the volume of antenatal care (ANC) attendees at the surveillance sites. The frequency of sentinel surveillance rounds among pregnant women should consider the data needs served by the surveillance and the available resources. HIV prevalence trend data from surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC is critical for countries to monitor the progression of their HIV epidemics, allocate resources effectively, and plan and evaluate HIV control and prevention interventions. To meet these data needs, surveillance among pregnant women should be conducted at regular intervals, approximately every two years. Conducting surveillance more frequently, such as annually, is unlikely to yield measurable changes in the epidemic and may not justify the additional resource expenditure. The sample size for sentinel surveillance is determined by the desired precision of prevalence estimates and the need to detect changes in prevalence over time. Accurate prevalence estimates maximize precision for a given cost. Sample sizes that are too small result in imprecise estimates, while excessively large sample sizes waste resources by providing more precision than necessary. Sample size requirements for obtaining a single prevalence estimate with a specified level of precision at the site level can be derived from published tables or statistical software. Precision is typically measured by the margin of error, defined as half the width of a 95% confidence interval. Narrower confidence intervals indicate more precise and reliable prevalence estimates. When calculating sample sizes, adjustments should be made to account for expected missing data. This ensures that the final sample size is sufficient to meet the surveillance objectives. Detecting statistically significant changes in HIV prevalence over time requires larger sample sizes than estimating prevalence at a single point in time. The smaller the change in prevalence to be detected, the larger the sample size required. In concentrated or low-level epidemics, detecting changes in prevalence at subnational levels may necessitate very large sample sizes. For young pregnant women aged 15–24 years, who are likely to have recently experienced sexual debut, HIV prevalence trends can serve as a proxy for recent infections. These trends are valuable for triangulating data to estimate HIV incidence. However, because sentinel surveillance is a non-probability design, data from different sites cannot be pooled to provide national or subnational estimates. If surveillance programs require prevalence estimates of a specified precision among young pregnant women, sample size calculations should be adjusted to ensure sufficient sampling of this subgroup. Methods such as inflation or oversampling can be used to achieve this, as described in detail in relevant appendices. Eligibility criteria for sentinel surveillance should be clearly defined. Inclusion criteria typically include women with confirmed pregnancies, aged 15–49 years, and attending their first ANC visit during the current pregnancy to avoid duplicate sampling. Exclusion criteria include women who have already attended an ANC visit during the current pregnancy or those outside the age range of 15–49 years. Eligible pregnant women are included regardless of their HIV status, antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, or whether they received an HIV test at their first ANC visit. Data collection methods for HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC should be economical, sustainable, and methodologically rigorous to ensure reliable HIV estimates with minimal bias. Surveillance programs should define which routine data tools will serve as the source of surveillance data. Ideally, a single data tool containing all necessary variables should be used. If multiple tools are required, they should be linked through a unique identifier to minimize complexity and ensure data quality. Standardized methods and data sources should be used across all sites to ensure comparability. All eligible pregnant women whose records are sampled should be assigned a unique surveillance code to facilitate data cleaning and management. This code should include information about the surveillance record and sampling, such as a site code followed by an ordinal number. Personnel involved in surveillance, including data collectors, supervisors, data managers, and statisticians, should have clearly defined responsibilities outlined in the surveillance protocol. Training should be conducted before each surveillance round, covering operational procedures, staff responsibilities, field protocols, and data security measures. If new procedures or personnel are involved, a field test of surveillance operations is recommended to identify challenges and provide hands-on training. In retrospective data collection, surveillance teams visit ANC sites after the surveillance period has ended to identify and sample records of eligible pregnant women. Consecutive sampling is a simple and effective technique for selecting records, starting from the first day of the surveillance period and continuing until the required sample size is reached. However, this method may result in samples from high-volume clinics being concentrated in time compared to those from lower-volume clinics. Surveillance programs should define specific methods for collecting data from routine site tools, ensuring methodological rigor, simplicity, and sustainability. Data collection methods may include manual transcription, electronic data entry, or digital imaging of routine site tools. Regardless of the method, data security and confidentiality must be maintained, and personal identifiers should not be captured unless necessary for data collection.
